title: Canada — entire open-record history spine
note: Dense chronological beats for multi-hour LIRIL documentary. FACT_CLASS only; each segment cites open gov / commission / statute / public social artifacts.

segments.title: Haudenosaunee Confederacy — Great Law of Peace
segments.narration: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy's Great Law of Peace is among the oldest continuous constitutional traditions on this continent. Clan mothers, council fire, and treaty protocols predate the Canadian Crown. Any film about Canadian government power that skips this order is not a history of the land — only a history of the later state.

segments.title: Anishinaabe, Cree, Dene, Inuit — plural sovereignty
segments.narration: Anishinaabe, Cree, Dene, Mi'kmaq, Inuit and dozens of other nations held distinct legal orders, trade routes, and seasonal territories. Confederation did not create law on empty ground. It layered a new machine over living systems the Crown later tried to erase by statute.

segments.title: Pacific and Plains polities — wealth, war, ceremony
segments.narration: Pacific Northwest potlatch economies and Plains buffalo diplomacy were not 'pre-politics.' They were systems of wealth, honour, and alliance. When Canada later criminalized potlatch and starved Plains nations after the buffalo collapse, it was attacking competing sovereignties — a fact later admitted in federal reports and courts.

segments.title: Cabot, Cartier, seasonal fisheries
segments.narration: John Cabot's voyages and Jacques Cartier's expeditions enter the written European ledger. Seasonal Basque and Breton fisheries already used these waters. Contact begins as resource economics, not settlement myth. Primary voyages are archived; interpretation must stay bound to those texts.

segments.title: Quebec founded — Champlain and alliances
segments.narration: Samuel de Champlain founds Quebec in sixteen oh eight. French survival depends on Indigenous alliances and knowledge. The colony is thin, militarized, and missionary. This is the seed of a dual legal tradition that Canada still has not resolved cleanly.

segments.title: Company of One Hundred Associates to royal colony
segments.narration: Corporate charters fail; the Crown takes New France as a royal colony. Seigneurial tenure, Catholic missions, and military governance define social order. The pattern of state-corporate fusion — company first, Crown second — will reappear in railways, pipelines, and consulting contracts centuries later.

segments.title: Great Peace of Montreal and the inland wars
segments.narration: The Great Peace of Montreal and decades of inland war show Indigenous nations as diplomatic principals, not props. French, British, and Haudenosaunee strategy intertwine. Later Canadian schoolbooks compressed this into a simple conquest story. The primary treaties and council records are more complex.

segments.title: Plains of Abraham — the Conquest
segments.narration: Quebec falls. Montreal follows. The Conquest is not the end of French society — it is a transfer of imperial title that leaves a people, a language, and a civil law under a new sovereign. Every later language crisis sits on this military fact.

segments.title: Royal Proclamation of 1763
segments.narration: The Royal Proclamation recognizes Indigenous title across vast interior lands and restricts private purchase. It is still cited in Canadian courts. When modern governments treat land as already emptied of title, they fight their own foundational document.

segments.title: Quebec Act — civil law and Catholic space
segments.narration: The Quebec Act restores French civil law and expands Catholic practice under the Crown — strategic loyalty politics as American revolution gathers. It is a bargain: keep the colony by accommodating identity. Canadian federalism never escapes this bargain's aftershocks.

segments.title: Loyalists and the Constitutional Act
segments.narration: American independence drives Loyalist migration. Upper and Lower Canada are created in seventeen ninety-one. Settler politics, land grants, and oligarchic councils — Family Compact and Château Clique — set the template for elite capture that reformers will later name.

segments.title: War of 1812 — border as identity forge
segments.narration: The War of eighteen twelve is remembered differently in the United States and Canada. For British North America it becomes a founding myth of survival. Indigenous allies — including Tecumseh's confederacy — pay costs the later Canadian state will rarely centre in school narratives.

segments.title: Rebellions — responsible government demanded
segments.narration: Armed rebellion in Upper and Lower Canada forces London to send Lord Durham. Responsible government becomes the reform demand against colonial oligarchy. The pattern is familiar: crisis, commission, partial reform that preserves core power.

segments.title: Durham Report — assimilation as policy
segments.narration: Durham recommends uniting the Canadas and absorbing French Canadians into British institutions. Assimilation is not a side comment — it is explicit state strategy. Later residential schools and language fights sit in this intellectual lineage.

segments.title: Act of Union and responsible government
segments.narration: The Act of Union merges Upper and Lower Canada. Responsible government arrives mid-century. Cabinets answer to elected assemblies — but the franchise is narrow, women are excluded, Indigenous peoples are constrained, and property rules the vote. Democracy is partial by design.

segments.title: Railways, debt, and the federal bargain
segments.narration: Canal and railway debt, American expansion anxiety, and legislative deadlock push elites toward a larger federation. Confederation will be sold as necessity and destiny. The film later asks whether the modern federal machine still serves citizens — or only the intermediaries.

segments.title: Charlottetown and Quebec Conferences
segments.narration: Colonial politicians bargain federalism in closed conferences. The public is not co-author. Indigenous nations are not co-sovereigns at the table. The deal is elite, imperial, and strategic — a fact the primary conference records do not hide.

segments.title: British North America Act in force
segments.narration: July first, eighteen sixty-seven. The Dominion exists. Sections ninety-one and ninety-two divide powers. Residual federal power and peace, order, and good government clauses will later stretch into emergencies and criminal law. Read the text — not the fireworks.

segments.title: Red River Resistance and Manitoba
segments.narration: Métis assert rights as Canada purchases Rupert's Land. Louis Riel's provisional government forces negotiation. Manitoba enters Confederation with bilingual and denominational school guarantees later eroded. The state's first western expansion is already a legitimacy crisis.

segments.title: Indian Act — the operating system
segments.narration: The Indian Act consolidates control over status, band governance, land, and movement. It is still in force, still amended, still litigated. Residential schools, pass systems, and potlatch bans ride this statute. This is not ancient history — it is continuous administration.

segments.title: Numbered Treaties — land for promises
segments.narration: Numbered Treaties open the Prairies to settlement under Crown terms. Oral and written accounts diverge on what was promised. Modern courts, specific claims, and treaty commissions keep reopening the record. The film holds both the state text and the Indigenous legal memory.

segments.title: Canadian Pacific Railway — nation and patronage
segments.narration: The CPR is sold as national destiny and built with public subsidy, Chinese labour, and political scandal. Pacific Scandal topples Macdonald temporarily. Infrastructure and corruption travel together — a ledger the Auditor General will later keep for other megaprojects.

segments.title: Northwest Resistance and Riel's hanging
segments.narration: The eighteen eighty-five Northwest Resistance ends with military force and Riel's execution. Métis and Cree leaders face the state. The hanging deepens fracture lines still visible in western and Indigenous politics. Primary trial records and petitions remain the standard.

segments.title: Residential schools — state policy of child removal
segments.narration: Residential schools are not accidents of private charity. They are funded and regulated as state and church policy to break family and language. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later documents cultural genocide. The film will return to those findings as legal anchors, not metaphors.

segments.title: Laurier boom — immigration and exclusion
segments.narration: Clifford Sifton's immigration machine fills the Prairies while Asian exclusion laws and head taxes show a racial hierarchy in statute. The Chinese head tax and continuous journey regulation are government instruments — not folk prejudice alone.

segments.title: Great War — conscription and sacrifice
segments.narration: Canada enters the First World War as a dominion and exits with national trauma, conscription crisis, and new industrial power. French-English splits harden. Veterans return to a state that will later fail many of them in housing and health — a pattern the modern Veterans Affairs record still documents.

segments.title: Persons Case — women as legal persons
segments.narration: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rules women are persons for Senate appointment. It is a constitutional milestone and a reminder that Canadian rights expansions often come from court fights, not elite generosity.

segments.title: Depression — Bennett, relief camps, On-to-Ottawa
segments.narration: Mass unemployment, relief camps, and the On-to-Ottawa Trek expose the thinness of federal social protection. Bennett's New Deal arrives late. Provincial and federal blame-shifting becomes a Canadian art form the film will see again in housing and health.

segments.title: Second World War — mobilization and internment
segments.narration: Canada mobilizes for total war. Japanese Canadian internment and property seizures are state policy later apologized for. The war also builds industrial capacity and expectations of full employment that seed the postwar welfare state.

segments.title: Postwar welfare architecture
segments.narration: Family allowances, unemployment insurance expansion, hospital insurance beginnings — the postwar settlement trades loyalty for security. Crown corporations and industrial policy expand. This is the high-water mark of state capacity the later neoliberal decades will erode while expanding coercive capacity elsewhere.

segments.title: Points system — race-neutral on paper
segments.narration: The points system retools immigration selection. Formally race-neutral criteria replace national-origin preferences. Outcomes still track global inequality and later temporary foreign worker expansions. The statute book is the evidence; political speeches are not.

segments.title: Medicare — federal cost-share and values fight
segments.narration: Federal medicare cost-sharing makes publicly funded physician care national. It is a rights and fiscal bargain. Later privatization pressures and MAID expansion will stress the same health system from opposite directions — both visible in Health Canada and provincial data.

segments.title: October Crisis — War Measures Act
segments.narration: The FLQ crisis triggers the War Measures Act. Civil liberties suspend in the name of order. The precedent of emergency power will be cited again in two thousand twenty-two under the Emergencies Act. Compare the statutes and the inquiries — do not rely on slogans.

segments.title: Constitution Act 1982 and the Charter
segments.narration: Patriation and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms transform litigation and politics. Section fifteen equality, section seven life liberty security, section one reasonable limits — the tools later MAID and public health cases will turn. Quebec does not sign. The constitutional wound remains.

segments.title: Free trade — FTA to NAFTA
segments.narration: Free trade elections realign Canadian politics. Economic integration with the United States deepens. Sovereignty debates become trade debates. Later digital and data sovereignty fights inherit this architecture.

segments.title: Oka — land defence under cameras
segments.narration: The Oka crisis puts Indigenous land defence on national television. It is not the first or last standoff. It forces a generation of Canadians to see that treaty and title disputes are present tense, not museum exhibits.

segments.title: Somalia Affair — military scandal and reform
segments.narration: The Somalia Affair forces public inquiry into Canadian Forces conduct and cover-up culture. Military justice and CFNIS later become permanent accountability files on this site. Scandals that do not produce structural change tend to recur.

segments.title: After September 11 — security state expansion
segments.narration: Anti-terrorism statutes, no-fly lists, and intelligence budgets expand after two thousand one. Oversight lags. The security state and the welfare state reverse trajectories — more surveillance capacity, thinner social capacity. Primary statutes and SIRC/NSICOP reports are the evidence.

segments.title: Sponsorship Scandal and Gomery
segments.narration: The Sponsorship Scandal and Gomery Inquiry document Liberal Party of Canada era misuse of public funds for political ends. It is a textbook case of patronage networks. The public accounts and inquiry transcripts remain online.

segments.title: Harper years — census, omnibus, Afghanistan
segments.narration: Long-form census cancellation fights, omnibus bills, Afghanistan combat, and accountability office creation coexist. The film does not romanticize any party. It tracks instruments of power: how statutes, budgets, and appointments move regardless of brand colour.

segments.title: TRC Final Report — cultural genocide finding
segments.narration: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documents residential schools as cultural genocide. Ninety-four Calls to Action become a public scoreboard governments still fail to complete on schedule. The finding is Canada's own commission speaking — not foreign propaganda.

segments.title: Carter and Bill C-14 — MAID legalized
segments.narration: Carter v Canada strikes down the absolute ban on assisted death. Bill C-14 creates medical assistance in dying under narrow conditions. Every later expansion starts from this hinge. Health Canada's annual reports will become the death ledger of the film.

segments.title: MMIWG Inquiry — genocide finding
segments.narration: The National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls finds genocide. Governments accept and then under-deliver. The film treats this as a second official genocide finding in four years — TRC and MMIWG — not as rhetoric.

segments.title: Pandemic powers and ArriveCAN
segments.narration: Emergency orders, border apps, and procurement explode. ArriveCAN becomes the Auditor General's emblem of cost overrun. Phoenix pay already proved payroll failure; ArriveCAN proves app failure. Same pattern, different decade.

segments.title: Bill C-7 — MAID expansion
segments.narration: Bill C-7 expands MAID beyond reasonably foreseeable natural death and sets the track for mental illness alone. Disability advocates warn. Hansard and committee evidence preserve the warnings. The death counts that follow are Health Canada's numbers.

segments.title: Emergencies Act — convoy and inquiry
segments.narration: The federal Emergencies Act is invoked for the first time. Banks freeze. The Rouleau commission later rules the threshold met — a finding critics dispute. Primary order-in-council text, commission transcripts, and court challenges are the record. Social media of officials and organizers is public secondary evidence.

segments.title: Hogue Commission — foreign interference
segments.narration: The Hogue Commission and NSICOP document foreign interference, naming the People's Republic of China as principal state actor and describing parliamentarians under foreign influence. Enforcement lags findings. That gap is the story.

segments.title: Media funding and concentration
segments.narration: Public funding of private media, CBC mandate fights, and ownership concentration reshape the information environment. Public social posts by broadcasters and influencers enter the OSINT graph. The film tracks money and amplification — not vibes.

segments.title: Transition year — open data still publishes
segments.narration: Cabinets change. The open data portals, Hansard, Health Canada MAID reports, and lobbying registry keep publishing. Social platforms remain public records of officials' claims. TENET5 freezes those streams daily so the film can point to timestamps, not memory.

segments.title: Lead-up complete — the present ledger
segments.narration: You have now walked the open-record path from nations before the Crown to this hour. The remaining acts drill multi-axis present files: MAID totals, housing, procurement, defence, and citizen remedies. The history was not decoration. It is the control group that proves the pattern is structural.
